text: Tally values from a small range, then print them in order.

When the values come from a **small range** (say 1 … 1000) but there are millions of them, tally them in a counting array and print each value as many times as it was seen. O(n + range), no comparisons at all (P1271).
Millions of numbers make input the bottleneck. Turn on fast IO (`fast` in your template), and never use endl per number.

title: 选择排序、冒泡排序、插入排序

text: The three O(n²) sorts, and what bubble sort counts.
For each position from the left, find the **smallest** value in the rest and swap it into place. At most n − 1 swaps, but always about n²/2 comparisons.
Walk the array, swapping **neighbours** that are out of order. After pass k the k largest values are in place at the end. Each swap fixes exactly one **inversion**: a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j].
Bubble sort swaps = inversions = the fewest neighbour swaps needed to sort (P1116). O(n²): fine for n up to a few thousand.
Keep a sorted prefix and slide each new value into place. **Fast when the data is almost sorted.**
All three are O(n²). Use them to understand or to count; use sort to sort.
Partition around a pivot, the k-th smallest, and merge sort for comparison.
Quicksort: pick a **pivot**, move smaller values left and bigger values right (partition), then sort the two sides the same way. About log n levels of O(n) work each.
The first element as pivot makes already sorted data O(n²). The middle element, or a random one, avoids that. P1177 includes such data on purpose; in practice just call sort.
To find only the k-th smallest, you need **just one side** after each partition: O(n) on average. The library does this as `nth_element`.
With 5 × 10⁶ numbers, slow input alone can time out: the two fast IO lines are required here (P1923).

Merge sort sorts each half, then merges two sorted lists by taking the smaller front value: always O(n log n). Taking from the right half jumps over everything left in the left half, which **counts inversions** in O(n log n).
std::sort, sort then scan, and sorting records by several keys.
`sort(a, a + n)` puts a[0] … a[n−1] in increasing order in O(n log n). After sorting, equal values sit next to each other, and the k-th smallest is at index k − 1.
The range is half open: first included, end excluded. For a 1 based array use `sort(a + 1, a + n + 1)`.
`unique` removes **adjacent** repeats, moving the kept values to the front, and erase cuts off the rest. It only works after sort makes all copies adjacent (P1059).
Small value range? A marking array does the same: `seen[x] = true`, then print every marked value in order.
Fewest items to reach a total: take the biggest first, which needs a decreasing sort (P2676).
"Do the gaps cover 1 … n − 1 exactly?" is a marking array (P1152).
Write the comparator as a **ladder**: compare key 1; if different, return that. Otherwise move to key 2, and so on. The last rung is usually the input order, an id you stored (P1093, P1068, P1786).
Need equal keys to keep input order? Add the id as the last key, or call `stable_sort` (P1104).
A comparator must be a strict order: `cmp(x, x)` must be false. Using `>=` or `<=` breaks sort, sometimes with a crash.
Cut off lines: sort, take the score at position ⌊m × 1.5⌋, then count everyone with a score ≥ that line, because ties at the line all pass (P1068).
Numbers too long for long long can still be compared: **more digits means bigger**; the same length means dictionary order (P1781).
C sorts with `qsort`. Its comparison returns a negative number, zero or a positive number, unlike C++'s true or false.
`return x - y;` can overflow for large values of opposite sign. `(x > y) - (x < y)` is safe.
